title: Buffett 1986 letter: owner earnings, managing by not getting in the way, and commodity insurance
summary: Buffett's 1986 shareholder letter covers hiring great managers and staying out of their way, capital allocation when good ideas are scarce, the Fechheimer deal and Berkshire's buying criteria, commodity insurance pricing, GEICO's cost moat, and the appendix on owner earnings versus the cash flow fallacy.

principles.text: Manage by hiring stars and staying out of their way; work only with people you like and admire.
principles.quote: They were managerial stars long before they knew us, and our main contribution has been to not get in their way.

principles.text: Capital allocation matters more the higher your returns and the more you retain.
principles.quote: the future results of a business earning 23% annually and retaining it all are far more affected by today’s capital allocations than are the results of a business earning 10% and distributing half of that to shareholders.

principles.text: Don't predict markets; be fearful when others are greedy and greedy when others are fearful.
principles.quote: we simply attempt to be fearful when others are greedy and to be greedy only when others are fearful.

principles.text: Value businesses on owner earnings, not GAAP earnings or cash flow that ignores maintenance capex.
principles.quote: But you shouldn't add (b) without subtracting ( c) : though dentists correctly claim that if you ignore your teeth they'll go away, the same is not true for ( c) .

principles.text: A low-cost position is a moat around a valuable castle; keep widening it.
principles.quote: The difference between GEICO’s costs and those of its competitors is a kind of moat that protects a valuable and much-sought-after business castle.

principles.text: In commodity businesses, profits attract capacity; the fix is less supply, not better behavior.
principles.quote: What’s needed is not more statesmen, but less corn.
